title: Language usage modulates the neural mechanisms of selective attention in bilinguals
abstract: Abstract The use of multiple languages modulates the neural mechanisms of selective attention, but it is unclear whether these adaptations require continuous engagement and active second language usage. Here we examined whether language usage shapes selective attention in bilingualism, and what neural processes this might engage. 48 highly proficient English-French bilinguals listened to naturalistic speech streams in their first or second language, paired with either linguistic or non-linguistic interference. Participants were matched on their L2 proficiency, but were either Active, Moderate, or Inactive users of their second language. The results revealed usage-related modulation of oscillatory activity in the alpha band, with increased power in Active and Moderate users and decreased alpha power in Inactive bilinguals, and behavioural comprehension accuracy mirroring this pattern of results. In contrast, there was no robust association between usage and perceptual tracking of speech, as captured by mTRF decoding of speech envelopes across frequency bands. Taken together, our findings suggest L2 usage may be modulating the neural mechanisms of auditory selective attention in bilinguals primarily through the top-down attentional allocation, without substantially altering the neural tracking of speech itself.
